claims.text: Yield onset in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is controlled by thermally activated screw-dislocation cross-slip rather than defect-mediated dislocation nucleation or phase transformation.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is an FCC solid solution.
The initial alloy is free of secondary phases.
Random distribution of the constituent atoms causes severe lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn.
Severe lattice distortion and chemical short-range order create high Peierls barriers for screw-dislocation motion.
The barriers to screw-dislocation motion necessitate thermally activated double-kink nucleation and cross-slip.
At low temperature, high lattice friction makes yield strength strongly temperature-dependent.
A small activation volume makes yield strength relatively insensitive to strain rate.
At higher temperatures, thermal assistance facilitates cross-slip and helps maintain strength.

High strain rates do not substantially change the yield point because thermal activation of the dislocation core, rather than dislocation velocity or free-surface nucleation frequency, is rate-limiting.
Yield strength decreases strongly as temperature increases from 77 K to 600 K.
Yield strength has only weak dependence on strain rate over the proposed test range.
A [111]-oriented crystal will have higher yield strength than a [100]-oriented crystal because screw motion on {111} planes requires higher resolved shear stress.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
Traditional FCC metals such as Cu and Ni are more strain-rate sensitive than FeNiCrMn.
Traditional FCC metals have lower Peierls barriers and different dislocation-mobility mechanisms than the hypothesized FeNiCrMn alloy.
Yield in traditional metallic single crystals is often controlled by dislocation nucleation.
Alloying additions capable of inducing a BCC phase would place the material outside the hypothesis boundary.
Polycrystallinity and significant grain-boundary effects can invalidate the proposed single-crystal mechanism.
Related HEA nanowire studies suggest that partial dislocations participate in twinning and deformation-induced phase transformation.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as having a random atomic distribution, while the mediator invokes chemical short-range ordering. These can coexist only if 'random' is qualified as lacking long-range order; as written, the descriptions are in tension.
